newsitem.title: FRANCE: French doctors end strike, airlines keep up action.
newsitem.headline: French doctors end strike, airlines keep up action.

text.p: France's junior hospital doctors voted on Tuesday to suspend a five-week strike against government plans to cap health spending but vowed to continue other forms of job action, their union said.

"Due to training imperatives, examinations and personal financial difficulties, the interns have decided to suspend their strike in its current form and to continue their actions in other ways," the ISNIH union said at a news conference.
The union called for a one-day strike on April 24 and said they would not bill their patients from that day.

Support for the strike had been eroding over the last week with one or two teaching hospitals abandoning the movement each day. Interns in Paris, Lille and Marseille decided to defy the national union and stay out on strike.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe welcomed the suspension of the strike, saying most of the doctors' demands had been met, and vowed to push ahead with a controversial overhaul of the French welfare system to rein in spending.
"We must stick to our course to succeed with our reforms," he told parliament, saying French health spending was 25 percent higher per capita than in Germany and 60 percent higher than in Britain.

By Monday night, only about nine hospitals had any junior doctors on strike compared to 24 at the height of the movement. The government estimated that only two had more than 50 percent of their junior doctors refusing to work.
The strikers wanted the government to delay or scrap plans to fine doctors if the region in which they work overshoots pre-set spending limits, regardless of individual practice.
The government refused to do away with the fines, but made them more individualised and established a seven-year moratorium on the penalties for new doctors setting up a practice.
"The doctors obtained satisfaction," Juppe said. "People mustn't say that we've introduced a system of collective responsibility which won't be individualised...It will be."

Meanwhile, striking cockpit crews at British Airways units TAT and Air Liberte forced the two French-based companies to cancel about 60 percent of their combined schedule on Tuesday, the companies said.
Unions are protesting over pay and conditions they say will be damaged by a merger of the two airlines.
